**What the GIL is.** The Global Interpreter Lock is a single mutex in CPython. It guarantees that exactly **one** thread executes Python bytecode at any given instant, even on a multi-core machine.

The GIL is a CPython implementation detail, not a requirement of the Python language spec. Jython and IronPython don't have one. CPython 3.13+ ships an experimental "free-threaded" build without it (PEP 703), but that build is not the default yet.

worst_places.quote: Separately from application code: the ASGI server (`uvicorn`) already knows how to finish in-flight HTTP requests on `SIGTERM` rather than cutting them off mid-response — but in an orchestrator (Kubernetes), one more thing matters: the **readiness** check should start failing immediately on receiving the stop signal, before the grace period even elapses, so new traffic stops arriving while old requests finish up.
worst_places.problem: Six unfamiliar concepts stack up inside one sentence (ASGI, SIGTERM, orchestrator, readiness check, grace period, traffic draining) with no example, no diagram and no code anywhere in the chapter. The whole 'senior polish' section works this way — 14 long paragraphs of pure prose. It is the one chapter in the range that names things instead of showing them, and it is the chapter a reader arrives at most tired.
worst_places.before: Separately from application code: the ASGI server (`uvicorn`) already knows how to finish in-flight HTTP requests on `SIGTERM` rather than cutting them off mid-response — but in an orchestrator (Kubernetes), one more thing matters: the **readiness** check should start failing immediately on receiving the stop signal, before the grace period even elapses, so new traffic stops arriving while old requests finish up.
worst_places.after:
The server itself already helps. When `uvicorn` receives `SIGTERM` (the "please stop" signal an orchestrator sends before killing a process), it finishes the HTTP requests already in flight instead of cutting them off mid-response.

But an orchestrator like Kubernetes needs one more thing from your app. Kubernetes gives a stopping process a grace period — a few seconds to wind down. During that window it keeps sending new requests unless something tells it not to. That something is the **readiness** check: it must start failing the moment the stop signal arrives, so new traffic goes to other replicas while the old requests here finish up.

```txt
SIGTERM arrives
  -> /readyz starts returning 503   (new traffic stops arriving)
  -> in-flight requests finish       (uvicorn handles this)
  -> pool.close(), process exits
```

worst_places.quote: **"Fully async endpoints" — what's actually changed here.** Since chapter 12 (aiosqlite) and chapter 13 (the first routes), all three endpoints were already `async def`. Technically, the "all endpoints async" box is already checked — but it's worth stating explicitly WHY that's still worth saying out loud: if even one handler in the app turned out to be synchronous and did a blocking call inside (a synchronous HTTP request, a heavy computation, a plain `time.sleep`), it would block the event loop's single thread for **every** other request the same process happens to be serving at that moment — exactly the cooperative model covered in chapter 12.

worst_places.after:
One synchronous handler is enough to stall the whole server. If a handler does a blocking call inside — a synchronous HTTP request, a heavy computation, a plain `time.sleep` — it holds the event loop's single thread, and **every** other request this process is serving right now waits for it. That is the cooperative model from chapter 12, seen from the server side.

Our three endpoints have been `async def` since chapters 12 and 13, so the box is already ticked. It is worth naming anyway, because nothing in FastAPI stops you from adding a synchronous handler later.

patterns: Untranslated or half-translated English leaks into the Russian text in five of the nine RU chapters, and in three of them the word is a Latin/Cyrillic hybrid that cannot be read at all: 'materializироваться' and 'materializируется' (18, twice in one sentence), 'транзitively' (17), plus whole English words dropped into Russian sentences — '— but сама функция' and '"as any hidden"' (10), '# ДО исправления — was в storage/...' (13), 'станет action неудобным' (12), 'которая resolves перед роутом' / 'resolving перед ним' (14). Add to that the English possessive 's grafted onto Russian ('log_command's wrapper', "Docker's HEALTHCHECK", "Node's Worker Threads") and one dropped space ('даётту же самую пользу', 15). These are not style choices; they read as an unfinished translation pass and they cluster in the two chapters a reader is most likely to skim (17-18).

The English version is systematically harder than the Russian, and the gap widens exactly where the material gets harder. Over-limit sentences: ch10 26%->41%, ch11 29%->51%, ch12 34%->50%, ch13 35%->47%, ch14 35%->47%, ch16 35%->51%. The cause is not extra content — it is that the RU sentence was already at the limit and the ~19% English expansion pushes it over, compounded by an idiom habit the RU does not have: 'earns its keep', 'pays for itself', 'the box is already checked', 'only half the journey', 'a dead end on both sides', 'nowhere to come from', 'a one-time box to tick', 'beefier version', 'gets in the way'. A B1-B2 reader on a phone loses one of these per paragraph.

Every chapter opens its theory sections correctly — a bolded lead sentence that states the point in plain words, then the caveats — but the caveat then gets stuffed back into the lead sentence as a parenthesis. The GIL definition (ch11) puts 40 words of caveats between subject and verb; the same shape recurs in ch13's Pydantic coercion note and ch14's exception-handler typing note. The fix is mechanical and does not lose a single fact: lead sentence, full stop, caveats as the next paragraph.

The difficulty ramp is supported everywhere except the last chapter. Chapters 10-17 each introduce one idea, show it in runnable code, and often show the real terminal output or the real mypy error it produced (ch11's three timed experiments and ch13's blank-text transaction bug are the strongest examples on the site). Chapter 18 breaks the pattern: it is 3155 words with zero code, 14 long paragraphs, and roughly fifteen tools and concepts named but never shown (SIGTERM, readiness vs liveness, grace period, token bucket, sliding window, contextvars, Alembic, asyncpg, Celery, RabbitMQ, slowapi, Fluentd/Vector/Promtail, Loki/ELK/CloudWatch). It is the one place in the range where the chapter assumes more than it teaches.

Course-wide terminology gaps that my chapters inherit rather than cause: CLI is used ~30 times across the whole course and expanded nowhere, in either language; SQL first appears in ch07 and is never expanded; ASGI, ORM, DTO, REST, TCP, ELK, RAM and CPU appear for the first time in chapters 13-18 and are expanded nowhere. Since a course is read in order, the fix is one expansion at the true first use (CLI in ch00, SQL in ch07, ASGI in ch14, DTO/REST in ch13, ORM in ch14, the rest in ch18).
notes: Two content defects found while auditing, reported for the owner rather than as readability findings: (1) ch15's exercise says create storage/users_storage.py but its worked solution imports `from ..storage import users as users_storage`, and ch16 imports `users_storage` — chapter 15's solution as printed will not import; (2) ch15 never shows the models/__init__.py and auth/__init__.py re-exports that its own imports depend on. Chapter 11 scores highest on D and E in the whole range (three experiments with real measured numbers) and lowest on F — its problem is purely sentence length in the EN version, not structure. Verdict is systemic-refactor rather than targeted-fixes only because of language: structure (C/D/E) is sound and should not be touched.
